# 3. Design Pressures {#sec-pressures-ch}

The developer, neighbor, farmer, buyer, and county do not want the same thing from a solar project. These are the **pressures**: forces with direction, conflict, and advocates. The axes say where a project sits; pressures explain how it got there. Naming them makes the actual disagreement arguable.

### 3.1 The pressures {#sec-pressures}

**Generation yield** — get the most electricity out of the ground. Panels packed close, tilted and turned to follow the sun, mounted low, covering the whole field. This is why a conventional array looks the way it does.

**Capital discipline** — build it for the least money. Standard racking, low mounting, no special site preparation, simple rectangles instead of awkward shapes. Anything unusual costs more, and this pressure asks why it is worth it.

**Operational simplicity** — keep it easy to run for the next twenty-five to forty years. Somebody has to manage that ground every one of those years, which pushes toward cover that is simple to mow, or gravel that does not grow at all. *It can push against capital discipline rather than with it: seeding natives costs more to put in and less every year after.*

**Agricultural continuity** — keep working land working. Panels high enough to get a tractor under, room to turn equipment at the end of a row, something growing underneath that is worth growing, and a contract the farmer can actually operate within.

**Restorative ambition** — leave the land better rather than merely less damaged, treating water, soil, habitat, and the farm's own finances as real goals alongside electricity [@hernandez2019]. It pushes for wider rows, mixed ground cover, a plan that covers all thirty years, and some choices made for the sake of what grows underneath. This is the pressure the document exists to advance. It is still one force among eight.

**Social license** — secure community acceptance and benefit. Acceptance requires early engagement that can change the design; benefit can include tax revenue, [community-benefit agreements](5-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit), payments, subscriptions, local hiring, and part-ownership. Money without a fair process does not reliably buy acceptance [@crawford2022; @ryder2023].

**Offtake conformity** — satisfy whoever is buying: the electricity, the renewable-energy credits, or the tax benefits. The design bends toward whatever the buyer scores. This is how a decision made in an office somewhere ends up determining what gets planted on one specific field.

**Decommissioning & reversibility** — leave little behind and keep open the option of farming again. It pushes for removable foundations, less digging, and funded [decommissioning](5-terminology.qmd#term-decommissioning).

![Eight competing forces resolving into one site design; the eighth is decommissioning & reversibility. Restorative ambition is shown in red because it is the pressure this lexicon exists to advance, but it is a force among forces, not a coordinate to be scored against.](../figures/fig_design_pressures.svg){#fig-pressures}

### 3.2 The conflicts worth naming {#sec-conflicts}

Left unnamed, these conflicts show up late: a stalled permit or a seed mix swapped for turf.

**Agricultural continuity vs. restorative ambition.** Should the ground under the panels grow food, or habitat? This is the American Farmland Trust / [ecovoltaics](5-terminology.qmd#term-ecovoltaics) argument. Requiring crops rules out pollinator plantings; choosing habitat gives up the farmland-protection case. Both sides are defending something real, which is why treating it as a misuse of words settles nothing.

**Operational simplicity vs. everything.** Gravel and herbicide are easy; diverse perennial cover is not. The maintenance bill decides many restorative designs.

**Offtake conformity vs. restorative ambition.** Buyers and scorecards can spread good ground-layer practice, but a rule written at a distance can also lock in a poor local fit for the term of a contract [@epri2021].

**Generation yield vs. restorative ambition.** Clearance, spacing, and crop shade tolerance interact. Vegetation can also cool modules, reduce dust, and lower panel-washing demand, so the two pressures occasionally align [@merheb2025].

**Capital discipline vs. operational simplicity.** Often mistaken for a single pressure. They split on what to plant, how high to mount, and how to get equipment in: cheap to build is frequently expensive to keep.

**Reversibility vs. restorative ambition.** Established habitat and rebuilt soil take years to create and resist clean removal.

**Social license vs. capital discipline.** Community benefit costs money but cannot substitute for fair process. Its cost should be calculated, not assumed: a biodiversity-conscious New York portfolio was only 0.17% above the least-cost case, although farmland preservation made other tradeoffs [@gallaher2026].

### 3.3 Design levers {#sec-levers}

The things a project can actually change fall into three groups.

*Structural — the hardware and its geometry:* mounting type (fixed, single-axis, dual-axis, vertical bifacial) · how high the panels sit · how far apart the rows are, and how much of the ground they cover · [pore-space](5-terminology.qmd#term-pore-space) configuration · module technology (monofacial, bifacial, semitransparent, spectrally selective).

*Land and ecology — the ground and how it is run:* what grows underneath · where on the parcel the array goes · whether the landscape holds a few large sites or many small ones · which ecological outcome is being aimed at · how the ground is managed across the project's life · how the array is operated (tracking schedule, curtailment) · how the edges are treated (setback, buffer, berm, fencing, [screening](5-terminology.qmd#term-screening)).

*Institutional — who owns it, who buys it, who benefits:* ownership and control · offtake structure · interconnection posture · which regulations and certifications apply · [community-benefit](5-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) structure (host or community-benefit agreement, PILOT and good-neighbor payments, community-solar subscription, co-ownership, decommissioning bond).

**Coupled levers.** Row spacing and ground layer are one decision: crops differ in shade tolerance [@weselek2019]. Edge treatment is both social-license and habitat design, with costs in land, shading, and farming room.

### 3.4 Levers across the transect {#sec-lever-matrix}

Levers change with scale. Read down a column for the choices available at that zone and across a row for how a lever changes. The table describes typical latitude; it does not prescribe dimensions or ownership.

| Lever | A1 · Farmstead | A2 · Field | A3 · Parcel | A4 · Landscape | A5 · Regional |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| ***Dominant [restoration mode](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*** | structure-led (by hand) | structure- / siting-led | siting-led (peak latitude) | management-led | management-led |
| **Structural** | | | | | |
| Mounting & clearance | ad hoc | crop-driven | tunable | standardized | commodity |
| Row geometry / GCR | set by footprint | crop- / machine-set | live tradeoff | cost-optimized | cost-set, minimal pore space |
| Module technology | off-the-shelf or bespoke | bespoke viable | some specialty | commodity | commodity only |
| **Land & ecology** | | | | | |
| Placement — siting latitude | parcel-bound | strategic choice begins | widest | narrowing | grid- / assembly-driven |
| Ground layer & management | hand-tended | farmer-managed | purpose-built | contract-enterprise | ranch-scale contract |
| Edge & screening | minimal, neighborly | setbacks appear | a social-license lever | major buffer element | screening + siting both |
| **Institutional** | | | | | |
| Ownership & control | owner-operator | landowner (± one lease) | multi-party / community-solar | developer capital | utility / IPP |
| Offtake & interconnection | behind-the-meter | distribution edge | distribution / community | sub-transmission; developer PPA | transmission / wholesale |
| Community-benefit structure | the household | good-neighbor scale | CBA / PILOT / subscription | PILOT + CBA customary | jurisdiction-scale |

: Design levers across the scale transect — what each lever usually looks like at each zone, and how much room is left in it. A description of what is typical and available, not a schedule of required values. {#tbl-lever-matrix}

Freedom shifts from hardware at the small end, to siting at A2–A3, to management and deal structure at scale. Read each cell as the latitude remaining in a lever, not a fixed fact about a zone.
